Holo4D: Holistic 4D Reconstruction as Geometric Control for Video Diffusion

Yushi Lan    Zeren Jiang    Koichi Namekata Affiliation: University of Oxford    Xingang Pan Affiliation: Nanyang Technological Universityhttps://nirvanalan.github.io/projects/holo4d    Chuanxia Zheng Affiliation: Nanyang Technological Universityhttps://nirvanalan.github.io/projects/holo4d    Andrea Vedaldi Affiliation: University of Oxford
Abstract

Synthesizing a monocular video from a new camera trajectory requires preserving the observed scene geometry and motion while completing regions that become newly visible. Feed-forward 4D reconstructors recover the structure of the observed scene, whereas video diffusion models provide a generative prior for completing unseen content. We introduce Holo4D, a video reshooting framework that uses reconstructed 3D trajectories as a holistic source-view 4D scaffold. We project these trajectories into the requested views and encode their geometry and source appearance to guide a pretrained video diffusion model. Together with the source video and target cameras, the scaffold grounds generation in reconstructed observations while leaving unsupported regions to the generative prior. Experiments demonstrate the value of trajectory-based conditioning for camera control and novel-view synthesis. The framework accommodates different 4D reconstructors without retraining the video generator, allowing it to benefit from future advances in source reconstruction. More details can be found in our project page.

11footnotetext: Equal contribution.

1 Introduction

Rendering a monocular video from a new camera trajectory would allow us to change the viewpoint of a recorded scene without changing the events it depicts [1]. For example, a camera moving around a walking person should reveal a different view of the same motion, rather than generate a different action or alter the surrounding scene. This requires both faithful reconstruction of observed content and plausible completion of surfaces that become visible only from the new viewpoint. The task therefore goes beyond recovering the geometry of the input frames: it must turn partial observations of a dynamic scene into a coherent video along a user-specified camera path.

Recent feed-forward reconstruction models provide an increasingly useful starting point. They estimate cameras, depth, and point maps directly from images and videos [2, 3, 4, 5], while 4D reconstruction systems also recover the trajectories of scene points over time [6, 7, 8, 9]. Together, these quantities describe the observed scene in a common spatial and temporal frame: camera motion can be separated from scene motion, and observations of a moving point can be linked across frames. However, reconstructing the observed scene does not by itself solve novel-view synthesis. Reprojecting its points into a new camera leaves holes where surfaces have never been observed [10], and inaccurate geometry can produce distortions as the viewpoint changes [11, 12]. The missing appearance must be inferred, rather than obtained by reprojection alone.

Video diffusion models offer the complementary ability to generate plausible appearance and motion from learned video priors [13]. Camera-controlled variants use these priors to synthesize new views, conditioned on camera embeddings or rendered source geometry [1, 14, 12]. Yet a realistic video need not preserve the geometry and dynamics of the particular scene being reconstructed. Combining reconstruction with generation is therefore not simply a matter of requesting a new camera pose: the generator also needs a representation of the scene that the camera is viewing. This motivates our central question: how should the geometry, appearance, and motion recovered from a source video be exposed to a video diffusion model?

An important part of this question is how the condition represents a scene over time. Lifting each frame independently with depth yields a sequence of point clouds, but does not explicitly specify which points correspond to the same moving surface in different frames. Vista4D [11] makes static scene content persistent by identifying static pixels and accumulating their observations in a common world frame. However, moving surfaces cannot be accumulated in the same way without accounting for their motion. Our starting point is that persistent 3D trajectories provide the required correspondence explicitly [6, 7, 8]. Specifically, a trajectory follows one scene point through time and associates its position with its observed appearance. A static point is the special case of a constant world-space trajectory, so static and moving points can use the same conditioning encoder.

We introduce Holo4D, a video reshooting framework that converts reconstructed 3D trajectories and their source appearance into geometric features for video diffusion (Figure 2). We call this scaffold holistic because it represents observed geometry, appearance, and motion jointly for static and dynamic points. Projecting these trajectories into the target cameras specifies where observed scene content should appear and how it should move. We use these projected trajectories to guide the video diffusion model, alongside source-video conditioning [15] and the requested camera trajectory [16]. The tracks guide observed content throughout denoising, while the video prior supplies plausible appearance in newly revealed regions.

This conditioning design has two useful properties. First, we inject track features along the channel dimension [17], providing geometric guidance without an additional rendered-video token stream [11]. Second, the scaffold uses explicit geometric quantities rather than reconstructor-specific features. Holo4D can therefore use any 4D reconstructor that provides the required geometry and trajectories [6, 8, 5, 18]. Our experiments show that replacing the upstream reconstruction can substantially improve camera adherence without retraining the video generator.

In summary, our contributions are threefold: (1) a holistic geometric scaffold that represents static and dynamic scene observations through persistent 3D trajectories with source appearance; (2) a conditioning design that combines source-video context with channel-wise injection of projected 3D trajectory features to guide novel-view generation; and (3) camera-adherence and held-out-view evaluations against strong baselines, analyses of reconstructor substitutions and trajectory perturbations, and demonstrations on robot videos.

2 Related Work

3D and 4D reconstruction.

Dynamic scenes can be reconstructed by fitting deformable radiance fields [19, 20, 21, 22] or time-varying Gaussian representations [23, 24, 25]. ViDAR [26] additionally uses a personalized diffusion prior to supervise per-scene Gaussian reconstruction. We instead condition a shared video generator on reconstructed geometry, without per-scene optimization.

Learned models recover point maps, cameras, and depth from images [27, 2, 4, 28, 29, 5] or accumulate observations over video [30, 3]. Video depth and dynamic-scene estimators provide geometry from moving-camera videos [31, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 37]. Recent 4D methods estimate dynamic point maps, motion, or persistent trajectories [38, 39, 8, 40, 41, 6, 7, 9], while 4DGT [42] predicts 4D Gaussians from posed videos. We use compatible geometric outputs as a scaffold for video reshooting.

Geometry-guided view synthesis.

Geometry-guided rendering aggregates source-view information to synthesize novel views [43, 44, 45, 46]. Ha et al. [46] also use temporal guidance and inpainting for multiview video. Our setting uses reconstructed 3D trajectories to condition video diffusion for reshooting a monocular video under large viewpoint changes.

Camera-controlled video generation.

Camera-conditioned diffusion models encode target views through poses or rays [47, 48, 49, 50, 51, 52, 53], and have been adapted to video reshooting [1, 54]. Explicit conditions instead ground generation in rendered source geometry [14, 12, 55] or warped observations [56]. Related methods generate multiview videos before Gaussian reconstruction [57], or render Gaussian features for sparse-view synthesis [44].

Vista4D [11] conditions on source video and rendered point clouds with temporally persistent static pixels. LaVR [58] uses latent reconstruction states, whereas our interface is defined by explicit geometric quantities rather than reconstructor-specific hidden features. Go-with-the-Track [17] conditions generation on reference images and reference-anchored 2D tracks for compositing and motion control, and also supports camera retargeting. Edit-by-Track [59] edits camera and object motion in a video by conditioning on paired source and target 3D point tracks. For video reshooting, Holo4D encodes 3D trajectory positions, source color, validity, and target-camera depth into geometric features, alongside the synchronized source video.

Diffusion models for geometry.

Diffusion priors also support geometry prediction, from monocular depth [60, 61] to video geometry and motion [37, 15, 9]. Gen3R [62] jointly generates appearance and geometric latents. VIST3A [63] couples a video generator to a reconstruction decoder, while Plan4D [64] further generates plannable 4D worlds by stitching video generators and reconstruction decoders. Holo4D instead takes reconstructed geometry as input and generates target-view RGB.

Video models for robots.

Video-generation backbones increasingly serve robot learning, e.g., as world action models [65]; Holo4D instead reshoots recorded robot videos from new viewpoints (Section 4.5).

3 Method

Given a source video Vsrc=(I0src,…,IN−1src)V^{\mathrm{src}}=(I_{0}^{\mathrm{src}},\dots,I_{N-1}^{\mathrm{src}}) and a target camera trajectory, Holo4D generates a video Vtgt=(I0tgt,…,IN−1tgt)V^{\mathrm{tgt}}=(I_{0}^{\mathrm{tgt}},\dots,I_{N-1}^{\mathrm{tgt}}) that shows the same scene and motion from the requested cameras. Source and target frames with the same index refer to the same scene time. In Figure 2, the top branch reconstructs persistent 3D trajectories from the source video, forming a 4D scaffold, projects them into the target cameras, and encodes them into target-aligned track features (Section 3.1). The bottom branch, a pretrained video diffusion model, generates the target video from the source video, the target cameras, and these features (Section 3.2).

3.1 Constructing a 4D scaffold

Reshooting a dynamic scene requires specifying where observed content should appear in each target frame and how its position changes over time. A video diffusion model conditioned only on the source video and target cameras [1] must infer this layout implicitly from appearance. Without an explicit scene representation, it struggles to preserve source-scene geometry and follow the requested camera under large viewpoint changes [58, 11]. To provide explicit geometric guidance, existing methods lift source frames into point clouds using estimated depth and render them from the target cameras [14, 12]. However, even when static points are accumulated across frames [11], independently reconstructed dynamic points do not explicitly establish correspondence between moving surfaces across frames. We therefore represent the source scene by persistent 3D trajectories [66], each carrying the appearance of a source observation.

To construct this scaffold, we use a 4D reconstructor ℛ\mathcal{R} to recover camera poses and point trajectories from the source video [6, 7, 8, 5, 18]. Each trajectory follows a scene point nn through its positions 𝐩n,j\mathbf{p}_{n,j} at successive frames jj and carries a color 𝐜n\mathbf{c}_{n}, sampled from the source frame qnq_{n} where the point was queried. We express these positions and the target cameras in the coordinate frame of the first source camera [27, 8], where static points have constant positions and moving points trace out their motion. Any reconstructor providing these trajectories and cameras can supply the scaffold.

To express the scaffold in the target views, we project each 𝐩n,j\mathbf{p}_{n,j} with the target intrinsics KjtgtK_{j}^{\mathrm{tgt}} and pose πjtgt\pi_{j}^{\mathrm{tgt}} of frame jj. This determines the point’s target-view pixel location and its target-camera depth dn,jd_{n,j}, both computed from the reconstructed 3D position. A validity flag vn,jv_{n,j} marks observations that are valid according to the upstream reconstructor and project inside the target image; it does not account for occlusion by other points. Each observation carries its frame index, position 𝐩n,j\mathbf{p}_{n,j}, depth dn,jd_{n,j}, validity vn,jv_{n,j}, and color 𝐜n\mathbf{c}_{n}. The color stays fixed along the trajectory, linking source appearance to the point’s reconstructed motion.

Finally, we convert the projected observations into a feature volume aligned with the target video. A sinusoidal encoding [67] followed by a shared MLP maps the attributes of each observation to a feature vector, which is scattered to its projected location on a target-view grid. Features of observations that fall into the same cell are combined by a channel-wise maximum, and an occupancy channel records which cells received any observation. A causal 3D convolutional adapter then brings this volume to the DiT token grid, producing the track features 𝐓\mathbf{T}; target tokens with no projected observations receive a learned null embedding. For a fixed target-video resolution and duration, the resulting feature volume has a size independent of the number of trajectories. Normalization, masking, and dataset-specific depth handling are given in Appendix B.

3.2 Conditioning video diffusion

The generator is a pretrained video diffusion transformer that combines source-video context, target-camera features, and the track features 𝐓\mathbf{T}. The VAE encodes the source video into latents xsrcx^{\mathrm{src}}, concatenated with the noisy target latents xτtgtx_{\tau}^{\mathrm{tgt}} along the width [15]. This keeps synchronized source and target frames at the same temporal index, whereas temporal concatenation [11, 1] places them at different indices. Learned domain embeddings distinguish the source and target halves. The text prompt enters through the backbone’s pretrained cross-attention.

The track features enter the transformer along the channel dimension, following Go-with-the-Track [17], rather than as an additional sequence of tokens. We place them on the target half of the sequence and extend 𝐓\mathbf{T} on the source half with the same learned null embedding used for unoccupied target tokens. Channel-wise injection leaves the self-attention sequence length unchanged, and our model achieves a 1.34×1.34\times denoising speedup over Vista4D (Table 24).

The projected trajectories already convey the target viewpoint through their image locations. To provide auxiliary camera information in regions without valid projected observations, we also encode the target cameras as Plücker rays [16] into camera features 𝐂\mathbf{C}. Source cameras establish the common reconstruction frame and are not separately embedded in the generator.

In the implementation, we inject the track and camera features before self-attention in every DiT block. Writing the hidden features of block ℓ\ell after normalization and timestep modulation as 𝐡(ℓ)\mathbf{h}^{(\ell)}, we compute the self-attention input as

𝐡^(ℓ)=W(ℓ)​[𝐡(ℓ);𝐓]+𝐂,\widehat{\mathbf{h}}^{(\ell)}=W^{(\ell)}[\mathbf{h}^{(\ell)};\mathbf{T}]+\mathbf{C}, (1)

where [⋅;⋅][\cdot;\cdot] concatenates channels and W(ℓ)W^{(\ell)} is a learned projection back to the hidden width. Following the zero-initialized conditioning principle of ControlNet [68], the projection initially preserves the hidden features and assigns zero weight to the track channels. The complete block layout is shown in Figure 11, with implementation details in Appendix B.

3.3 Training and inference

A training example consists of a source video with 3D trajectory annotations, target cameras, and the target video seen from those cameras. The trajectory annotations are required to construct the conditioning features 𝐓\mathbf{T} and are obtained from an upstream reconstructor or, where available, dataset ground truth. We encode the target video into latents xtgtx^{\mathrm{tgt}} and corrupt them with Gaussian noise ϵ\epsilon as xτtgt=(1−τ)​ϵ+τ​xtgtx_{\tau}^{\mathrm{tgt}}=(1-\tau)\epsilon+\tau x^{\mathrm{tgt}}, where τ∈[0,1]\tau\in[0,1] is the diffusion time, distinct from the video frame index; the source latents stay clean. The generator u𝜽u_{\bm{\theta}} is trained to predict the velocity of this interpolation with the rectified-flow objective [69]

ℒFM=𝔼⁡[‖u𝜽​(xτtgt,τ,xsrc,𝐓,𝐂)−(xtgt−ϵ)‖22],\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}=\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|u_{\bm{\theta}}(x_{\tau}^{\mathrm{tgt}},\tau;x^{\mathrm{src}},\mathbf{T},\mathbf{C})-(x^{\mathrm{tgt}}-\epsilon)\right\|_{2}^{2}\right], (2)

where the expectation is over training examples, noise, and diffusion time; auxiliary conditions are detailed in Appendix B. Only the target latents are supervised; no geometry is predicted.

At test time, we reconstruct the source video, build 𝐓\mathbf{T} and 𝐂\mathbf{C} for the requested cameras, and integrate the learned velocity from noise to target latents, which the VAE decodes into the output video. Videos longer than the training window are generated window by window (Section 4.5 and Appendix B).

3.4 Training details and datasets

We initialize from Wan2.1-T2V-14B [70] and train on 4949-frame videos for 1515k steps at 144×256144{\times}256, followed by 4.54.5k steps at 384×672384{\times}672. AdamW [71] uses learning rates 1×10−51{\times}10^{-5} and 2×10−52{\times}10^{-5} and effective batch sizes 88 and 3232 for the two stages, respectively. We train conditioning modules and DiT self-attention, keeping pretrained cross-attention and feed-forward layers frozen [72].

Datasets.

We train on a mixture of synthetic multiview videos of dynamic scenes [73, 74, 1], real videos of static scenes [75, 76], and synthetic static-scene sequences [77, 78]. For dynamic scenes, source–target pairs come from synchronized multiview videos. For static scenes, we form source–target pairs from different chunks of the same monocular video, similar to 4Real-Video-V2 [79]; temporal synchronization is unnecessary since the scene is static. This mixture covers both scene motion and camera motion, with estimated or ground-truth 3D trajectory annotations; dataset names, sampling weights, and annotation sources are given in Appendix C.

To expose the generator to imperfect and incomplete conditions, the second training stage varies trajectory density and query-frame sampling and applies mild geometric perturbations. Module dimensions and augmentation settings are specified in Appendix B.

4 Experiments

We evaluate camera control and novel-view synthesis (Sections 4.2 and 4.3), analyze geometric conditioning (Section 4.4), and demonstrate robot-video applications (Section 4.5).

4.1 Experimental setup

Baselines.

We compare Holo4D with several representative state-of-the-art methods, including ReCamMaster [1], TrajectoryCrafter [14], EX-4D [55], Gen3C [12], and the concurrent Vista4D [11]. ReCamMaster is a camera-only baseline: it conditions on the source video and the target cameras. The others are rendered-geometry baselines: they also render source geometry from target cameras; Vista4D keeps static geometry persistent across frames.

Evaluation datasets.

For camera control, we select 5050 DAVIS [80] clips and randomly sample two target camera trajectories per clip, and also evaluate on Vista4D’s released 110110-trajectory benchmark. Five iPhone/DyCheck scenes [81] provide synchronized held-out views, while held-out Syn4D [73] scenes provide exact target RGB and geometry. For each metric, all methods are evaluated at the same resolution; detailed protocols are in Appendices D, F and I.

4D scaffold reconstruction.

Our default source reconstructor ℛ\mathcal{R} is 4RC [6]. We also test two-stage 4D reconstruction from 3D geometry and 2D tracking, as used for annotation in MolmoMotion [82], by combining VGGT-Ω\Omega [5] with CoWTracker [18]. For this two-stage backend, we optionally use GMOS [83] to hold background points fixed in 3D while preserving foreground motion.

Inference.

For Holo4D, we query points in the first source frame and use 5050 denoising steps on DAVIS and iPhone; Syn4D settings are in Appendix I. Baselines use their released sampling settings.

4.2 Quantitative comparisons

Novel-view video synthesis.

Table 1 compares generated views with synchronized iPhone recordings. PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS score full images; masked (“m”) variants score only co-visible pixels.

With the two-stage backend, Holo4D obtains the best PSNR (13.2013.20 dB) and LPIPS in both forms, ahead of EX-4D and Vista4D; EX-4D leads in SSIM, and our 4RC variant is second in LPIPS. Both variants use the same generator without retraining, illustrating the effect of the source geometry and its preprocessing. Figure 4 shows visual comparisons; Table 18 compares with per-scene ViDAR.

Camera control accuracy.

Table 2 compares camera control on 100100 DAVIS video–trajectory pairs using VGGT-Ω\Omega camera recovery [5]. ATE measures trajectory error; RPE-T and RPE-R measure adjacent-frame translation and rotation errors. Translation metrics use 5454 pairs; rotation uses all 100100. Holo4D has the lowest trajectory and translation errors of all methods and lower rotation error than all rendered-geometry baselines. With both methods using 4RC source reconstruction on DAVIS, Holo4D reduces ATE by 54%54\% and RPE-T by 33%33\% compared with the concurrent Vista4D. ReCamMaster attains a slightly lower rotation error (0.099∘0.099^{\circ} versus 0.102∘0.102^{\circ}) but the largest trajectory error of all methods, consistent with outputs that stay close to the source viewpoint.

Video quality.

Table 2 reports five VBench [84] dimensions on the same DAVIS videos. Holo4D scores highest on imaging quality and, among rendered-geometry baselines, on subject and background consistency; it also exceeds Vista4D on aesthetic quality, with a marginally lower temporal-style score. ReCamMaster’s high consistency accompanies the largest trajectory error: consistency alone does not establish camera fidelity. FVD computed against source videos can reward copying the input despite failed camera control. We therefore report FVD only on Syn4D, using ground-truth target-view videos as references; Holo4D achieves the lowest FVD with ground-truth source geometry (Table 3).

Novel-view synthesis on synthetic scenes.

Syn4D provides exact target views and source geometry, removing reconstruction error from the comparison. With ground-truth source depth and cameras for rendered-geometry baselines and 3D trajectories for Holo4D, Holo4D leads on all camera and image metrics (Table 3). With 4RC estimates on a separate 3232-pair set, Holo4D leads on camera errors and LPIPS, while camera-only ReCamMaster leads on PSNR and SSIM (Table 19). Test scenes are held out, but Syn4D is in our training mixture and the baseline checkpoints are not adapted to it; real-video evaluations test beyond our training datasets.

Depth consistency of generated views.

We reconstruct generated-video depth and compare it with exact target depth on Syn4D (Table 20). Holo4D has the lowest AbsRel and highest δ1\delta_{1} under both output reconstructors, VGGT-Ω\Omega and 4RC; VGGT-Ω\Omega AbsRel falls from Vista4D’s 0.6280.628 to 0.4230.423. On iPhone, with reconstructed target-video depth as a pseudo-reference, our two-stage variant also has the lowest AbsRel under both reconstructors, supporting improved generated-view geometry.

Comparison with per-scene optimization.

ViDAR [26] takes about 55 h 1818 min per iPhone scene on an A6000 for optimization; Holo4D needs no scene-specific optimization. Given the same first 4949 source frames, our two-stage variant has higher PSNR and lower LPIPS, including masked variants, while ViDAR has higher SSIM (Table 18); ViDAR natively uses the full sequence.

Sampling cost.

Because the track condition enters along channels, Holo4D adds no tokens to self-attention, whereas Vista4D appends a rendered-video token sequence. In a matched comparison at 384×672×49384\times 672\times 49 with 5050 denoising steps on one H200, Holo4D achieves a 1.34×1.34\times denoising speedup (7.397.39 versus 9.899.89 s) at similar peak memory (Table 24); end-to-end time per video is nonetheless similar (570.9570.9 versus 581.9581.9 s), since loading, conditioning, decoding, and writing offset the gain. Source reconstruction is paid once per input video and reused across target trajectories (8.88.8 s for 4RC and 11.811.8 s for the two-stage backend in warm A6000 runs, Table 24); only projection and encoding are redone per trajectory.

4.3 Qualitative comparisons

Figure 3 shows a restaurant side dolly and a car-following shot from Vista4D’s benchmark. ReCamMaster stays close to the source framing; TrajectoryCrafter and Gen3C change or duplicate people and, like EX-4D, lose the car. EX-4D also leaves large holes. Vista4D turns the foreground diner toward the new camera and omits the car’s rear window (red boxes and insets). Holo4D preserves the diner’s orientation, rear window, and lights while following the requested path; Tables 2 and 6 quantify camera accuracy, and Figure 16 shows two further trajectories. On iPhone (Figure 4), Holo4D preserves the person and scene objects at the target viewpoint.

4.4 Analysis of the geometric scaffold

Conditioning design. Table 4 compares conditioning variants trained with the same stage-1 recipe (1515k steps at 144×256144\times 256). Removing the per-track color raises ATE by 44%44\% even though the source video remains available, so track-attached appearance is not redundant with the video. Removing target depth has a smaller effect, likely because depth follows from the 3D positions and target cameras. Adding rendered RGB and mask features to the track features improves none of the camera metrics, favoring trajectory-only conditioning for camera control at this training budget.

Reconstruction backends. The same generator accepts 4RC, V-DPM, and VGGT-Ω\Omega paired with Open-D4RT or CoWTracker as ℛ\mathcal{R} without retraining (Table 5), and the backends trade off differently: the CoWTracker variant gives the best ATE, PSNR, and SSIM, V-DPM the best rotation error, and 4RC the best LPIPS. Ground-truth geometry improves all five metrics, leaving room for better reconstructors.

Trajectory accuracy. To isolate the effect of geometric error, we add Gaussian noise to ground-truth tracks, with standard deviation α\alpha times that of the source tracks along each axis, keeping all other inputs fixed. Even mild noise (α=0.1\alpha=0.1) triples rotation error (0.073∘0.073^{\circ} to 0.221∘0.221^{\circ}) and degrades SSIM and LPIPS although the clean source video remains available, showing that clean video context does not fully compensate for geometric error. ATE does not grow beyond α=0.1\alpha=0.1; independent alignment of each recovered camera trajectory can absorb part of the error. Full results and protocols are in Appendices G and I.

Rotation control with accurate geometry.

With ground-truth source geometry on nine held-out Syn4D clips, Holo4D has lower error on all five camera metrics than Vista4D, including source-aligned rotation (0.242∘0.242^{\circ} versus 0.372∘0.372^{\circ}; Table 14). Replacing GT with 4RC estimates on the same clips and checkpoint raises this error to 0.931∘0.931^{\circ} but barely changes relative rotation error (0.051∘0.051^{\circ} to 0.055∘0.055^{\circ}), consistent with an orientation offset despite similar local motion. Accurate relative motion therefore does not guarantee the requested viewpoint.

Camera control on Vista4D trajectories. On Vista4D’s 110110 trajectories (Table 6), Vista4D uses its released Pi3 geometry and reprojections, while Holo4D uses 4RC or the two-stage backend (protocols in Appendix E). With scalar-depth-aligned 4RC geometry, Holo4D has similar ATE, lower RPE-T and Pi3 translation error, but higher rotation errors than Vista4D. Substituting the two-stage backend cuts rotation error by 74%74\% under VGGT-Ω\Omega and 59%59\% under Pi3 (14.98∘14.98^{\circ} to 6.098∘6.098^{\circ}), improves ATE and RPE-T, and slightly raises Pi3 translation error. Pi3 rotation remains above Vista4D’s 4.169∘4.169^{\circ}. The comparison with Vista4D does not isolate the generator.

4.5 Robot videos

Zero-shot reshooting.

Holo4D-14B is trained without robot videos, yet reshoots DROID manipulation episodes and humanoid-robot clips without fine-tuning (Figures 5 and 17).

Long-video rollout.

We generate overlapping 4949-frame windows: the first with Holo4D-14B, then with an image-to-video continuation model conditioned on the last generated frame (Appendix B). The continuation model trains on OmniWorld-DROID, so later windows are not zero-shot. Figure 6 qualitatively shows consistent appearance across two window boundaries in a 196196-frame episode.

Transfer to robot policy learning.

We initialize Fast-WAM’s [65] 3030 video self-attention blocks from a 5B Holo4D variant (Appendix L) and train on LIBERO [86] alongside a matched Wan2.2-initialized control (Table 7). Results are mixed: LIBERO has few tasks and is near saturation (95.60%95.60\% vs. 96.45%96.45\%), leaving little room to distinguish the two. On LIBERO-plus [87], Holo4D gains 1.291.29 percentage points overall, mainly under background-texture (+7.1+7.1) and lighting (+3.9+3.9) perturbations, but loses on the spatial suite. Camera-viewpoint perturbations remain hard for all checkpoints (single seed). Whether novel-view training helps embodied policies remains open and merits further study.

5 Conclusion

Holo4D guides video diffusion with persistent 3D trajectories that carry source appearance, leaving regions beyond the scaffold to the generative prior. It achieves the lowest trajectory and translation errors on DAVIS and the best PSNR and LPIPS on iPhone with the two-stage backend, and works with different reconstructors without retraining; it remains sensitive to geometric error, incomplete source coverage, and difficult camera trajectories.

Future work.

Since video generators are general-purpose vision learners [88], one model could jointly perform 4D reconstruction and novel-view synthesis so that both improve together. Querying trajectories in every source frame, not just the first (e.g., UniQueR [89]), would cover later-appearing content; stronger base models such as MiniMax H3 [90] should improve visual quality.

Appendix A Changes from the Submitted Version

The task, title, and central idea are unchanged: Holo4D exposes source-view 4D reconstruction to a pretrained video diffusion model to reshoot a monocular video along a new camera path. After review, we simplified conditioning, retrained the model, and expanded evaluation. Changed checkpoints, resolutions, and camera evaluators preclude direct comparison with submitted numbers. Table 8 summarizes the differences; the main one is that the rendered RGB-D (depth) branch is removed and only the 3D-track branch is kept. Figure 8 reproduces the submitted pipeline, and Figures 10, 8 and 10 reproduce its qualitative results.

Submitted conditioning.

The submitted paper described four conditioning signals: the source video, a hybrid RGB-D cache, target-camera Plücker rays, and 3D-track tokens. A 3D-motion threshold separated static and dynamic pixels. Static pixels were fused from K=7K=7 keyframes selected by farthest-point sampling over camera positions and viewing directions; dynamic pixels came from the synchronized source frame. The described design merged their renders by z-buffer selection into target-view RGB, normalized depth, and validity. Track tokens encoded 3D trajectory positions and were fused with the RGB-D tokens. The actual submitted 14B DAVIS and iPhone results used multiframe softsplat RGB-D conditioning; the 1.3B DAVIS results used single-frame z-buffer conditioning. Both included 3D tracks.

Final conditioning.

This version removes the rendered RGB-D branch, which supplied target-view RGB, depth, and validity, and keeps only the 3D-track branch, together with the source video and target-camera rays (Section 3, Figure 2 versus Figure 8). Observations encode source color and target-camera depth (Equation 3); validity combines upstream validity with in-image projection, without the occlusion test of z-buffer visibility. Since a static point is a trajectory with a constant position, the static–dynamic threshold and keyframe selection are no longer needed. In a controlled stage-1 comparison, adding rendered RGB and masks to the trajectory features did not improve camera control (Table 4); Tables 15, 16 and 17 report further comparisons with rendered conditioning from earlier checkpoints. Track features enter every DiT block along channels and add no attention tokens (Appendix J).

Model and training.

The submission reported a 14B model built on Wan2.1-I2V-14B and a 1.3B model built on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B, both trained at 144×256144\times 256 and 288×512288\times 512. The main results in this version use a 14B model initialized from Wan2.1-T2V-14B and trained at 144×256144\times 256 and then 384×672384\times 672, with a revised data mixture (Appendices B and C). Early 1.3B checkpoints appear only in the conditioning study of Table 15, not as main results. The submission also probed target-view depth with a separately trained head on intermediate VAE decoder features; this version omits that probe and evaluates depth reconstructed from generated RGB videos (Table 20).

Evaluation.

Cameras of generated videos are now recovered with VGGT-Ω\Omega instead of ViPE (Appendix D). Video quality on DAVIS is measured with VBench; FVD is reported on Syn4D, where target-view references exist. New evaluations cover Vista4D’s 110110-trajectory benchmark (Appendix E), Syn4D with exact target RGB and geometry (Appendix I), per-scene optimization with ViDAR (Table 18), alternative source reconstructors used without retraining, noise injected into the trajectories (Tables 5 and 21), and runtime (Appendix J). Several of these were requested by reviewers and first reported in the author response.

Robot videos.

Section 4.5 is new. It shows zero-shot robot-video reshooting with Holo4D-14B, long-video generation using a continuation model trained partly on robot videos (Appendix B), and Fast-WAM policy learning initialized from a 5B Holo4D variant (Appendix L).

Presentation.

The abstract, introduction, and method are rewritten for trajectory-based conditioning, and all figures are redrawn.

Submitted visual results.

For reference, Figures 10, 8 and 10 reproduce the qualitative results of the submitted version: the frames are unchanged and are laid out in the format of the current figures. They come from the submitted checkpoints with rendered RGB-D and track conditioning; the 14B DAVIS and iPhone results used multiframe softsplat rendering. The corresponding results of the final model are in Figures 3, 4, 15 and 16.

Appendix B Implementation Details

GMOS preprocessing.

For the DAVIS two-stage backend, GMOS [83] separates query-frame background and foreground identities. Background points are fixed at their query-frame 3D positions and kept valid; foreground points retain their depth-lifted trajectories and validity. Both enter the same track encoder, without additional mask channels or a separate foreground/background branch.

Source–target alignment.

Following the dynamic point-map notation of V-DPM [8], Pisrc​(tj,π0src)​(u)P_{i}^{\mathrm{src}}(t_{j},\pi_{0}^{\mathrm{src}})(u) denotes the position at video time tjt_{j} of the point observed at pixel uu in source frame ii, expressed in the first source-camera frame. For point nn, queried at pixel unu_{n} in source frame qnq_{n}, the main text uses 𝐩n,j=Pqnsrc​(tj,π0src)​(un)\mathbf{p}_{n,j}=P_{q_{n}}^{\mathrm{src}}(t_{j},\pi_{0}^{\mathrm{src}})(u_{n}) and 𝐜n=Iqnsrc​(un)\mathbf{c}_{n}=I_{q_{n}}^{\mathrm{src}}(u_{n}). Source and target latents are concatenated along width, so the two views retain the same temporal indices. The source half receives null track features; projected track features guide the target half. Source cameras define the common geometric frame, while target cameras determine projection and the Plücker-ray condition. No separate source-camera rays are encoded.

Backbone.

We initialize from Wan2.1-T2V-14B [70], which has 4040 DiT blocks and a 1616-channel video VAE with spatial compression 88 and temporal compression 44. We fine-tune self-attention and the new conditioning modules, while keeping cross-attention and feed-forward layers frozen. The new modules comprise the source–target domain embedding, query-frame indicator embedding, track encoder and injectors, and camera adapter and projectors.

Track encoding.

For point nn in video frame jj, the input attributes are

𝐳n,j=[t¯j;𝐩~n,j;vn,j;d~n,j;𝐜n]∈ℝ9.\mathbf{z}_{n,j}=\left[\bar{t}_{j};\;\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{n,j};\;v_{n,j};\;\widetilde{d}_{n,j};\;\mathbf{c}_{n}\right]\in\mathbb{R}^{9}. (3)

The frame index is normalized as t¯j=j/max⁡(N−1,1)\bar{t}_{j}=j/\max(N-1,1). Tildes denote normalized position and depth: each position coordinate is scaled using its per-sample minimum and maximum over all point identities and frames, then zeroed for invalid observations. Depth is scaled by its per-sample maximum. Validity combines the upstream track mask with valid projection into the target image; it is not an exact target-view occlusion test. Depth is the point’s target-camera zz coordinate, rather than a separate depth-image condition. Source color is sampled at the query frame and held fixed along the track. We discard identities invalid in every target frame, then subsample or pad to M=H​WM=HW identities, with padded rows inactive. At 384×672384\times 672, this gives M=258,048M=258{,}048.

A sinusoidal encoding and MLP map observations to 3232-dimensional features. Target-view projection determines where to scatter these features, with channel-wise maximum aggregation and an occupancy indicator. Temporal patchification repeats the first frame to respect the VAE’s causal layout, then applies a 3D convolution with kernel and stride (4,p,p)(4,p,p), where pp is the spatial downsampling factor, followed by one causal residual block and projection to 156156 channels. The resulting features match the DiT token grid. Empty tokens use a learned, zero-initialized embedding. The source half of the width-concatenated latent sequence receives null track tokens.

Camera conditioning.

One shared camera encoder produces the target-camera features used in every DiT block. These features are repeated along width to match both source and target tokens. This repetition does not introduce source-camera rays; explicit source-camera rays would be compatible with this design but are untested. Each block has its own track concat–projection and camera output projector. Camera rays use the Plücker convention [𝐨×𝐝,𝐝][\mathbf{o}\times\mathbf{d},\mathbf{d}]. Pixel unshuffle and a 2D convolution patchify the ray map; a zero-initialized pointwise 3D convolution maps its six channels to the DiT width. Within each block, track concatenation and projection follow normalization and timestep modulation. The camera feature is then added before self-attention, whose output passes through an identity-initialized camera projector and the gated residual connection. Cross-attention and the feed-forward sublayer follow.

Query-frame indicator.

A query-frame indicator identifies the source frames used to initialize trajectories. A binary sequence is one at the selected query frame and zero elsewhere; each value is broadcast over the image and repeated across three channels for encoding with the video VAE. The resulting control latents occupy the source half of the width-concatenated input, with zeros on the target half. A separate, zero-initialized Conv3D patch embedding maps these control latents to the hidden width, and its output is added to the video patch embeddings before the DiT blocks. This input addition uses neither the per-block track concat–projection nor a concatenation with the RGB latent channels.

Training.

Stage 1 uses 4949 frames at 144×256144\times 256 for 15,00015{,}000 steps, with effective batch size 88 and learning rate 1×10−51{\times}10^{-5}. Stage 2 continues the same checkpoint to step 19,50019{,}500 at 384×672384\times 672, with effective batch size 3232 and learning rate 2×10−52\times 10^{-5} on 3232 GPUs using FSDP [91]. Both stages run on NVIDIA GH200 GPUs for about 2424 hours each. Both stages optimize RGB flow matching. No geometric-conditioning dropout is used; text-conditioning dropout is 0.10.1.

Long-video rollout.

We extend generation beyond the 4949-frame training window by following Vista4D’s window-by-window inference [11]. (i) Split the source into 4949-frame windows with one-frame overlap: kk windows cover 49+48​(k−1)49+48(k-1) frames. Pad the last window by repeating its final source frame. (ii) Reconstruct each window independently using the backends specified below, querying trajectories at its first frame; identities are not shared across windows. Register each reconstruction to the first window through the shared boundary frame, holding its source camera fixed while fitting a scale to the shared point map. Use the corresponding segment of the requested target-camera path. (iii) Generate the first window with Holo4D-14B (step 19,50019{,}500), conditioned on the source video, tracks, and cameras. (iv) Generate later windows with an image-to-video continuation model using the same conditions plus the previous window’s last generated frame. This shared boundary image is never a source or ground-truth frame. Remove duplicate boundary frames and padding when stitching.

The continuation model uses a Wan2.1-I2V-14B [70] backbone and the stage-1 Holo4D-14B track and camera modules. Its image condition enters through the first-frame VAE latent and CLIP image feature. During training, this is the first ground-truth target frame, dropped with probability 0.30.3 and noised at level 0.050.05. Training proceeds at 144×256144\times 256 from step 15,00015{,}000 to 19,00019{,}000, then at 384×672384\times 672 to step 22,50022{,}500, with effective batch size 3232 and learning rate 2×10−52\times 10^{-5}. The mixture is MultiCamVideo (22.5%22.5\%), Syn4D (30%30\%), DL3DV (15%15\%), MVS-Synth (7.5%7.5\%), and OmniWorld-DROID [92, 85] (25%25\%); unlike Holo4D-14B, this model has seen robot videos. Window 1 uses 4RC for DROID and the two-stage backend for humanoid clips; later windows use 4RC without GMOS. Each 4RC reconstruction uses all 4949 source frames. All windows use 5050 denoising steps, CFG 55, shift 55, and seed 4242 (Figures 6 and 18).

Condition augmentation.

Stage 2 perturbs geometric conditions with probability 0.250.25. The configured track-offset and temporal-jitter standard deviations are 0.0050.005 and 0.0020.002; image-coordinate noise ratio is 0.100.10. Frame-depth jitter, depth offset, and depth-scale perturbation use 0.200.20, 0.0020.002, and 0.0030.003, respectively. RGB perturbations use 0.003/0.0060.003/0.006, and mask augmentation probability is 0.100.10. Sparse-track sampling is enabled with probability 0.50.5, with strides 22, 44, or 88; multi-query sampling uses two or three query frames with probability 0.50.5.

Appendix C Training Data

Table 9 reports sampling weights for both training stages. The first stage uses a broad mixture of synthetic and real, static and dynamic scenes; the second concentrates on four datasets at higher resolution. Geometry supplies conditions for RGB generation, not auxiliary prediction targets. Syn4D’s flying_group and MVS-Synth sequence 0000 are excluded from both stages. Weights are rounded to two decimal places; category totals are computed before rounding.

Stage 1 combines Syn4D and two equally weighted Kubric subsets for dynamic scenes, together with real static scenes from DL3DV and RE10K and synthetic static scenes from MVS-Synth and TartanAir. Each Kubric subset contributes approximately 6.33%6.33\% of the stage-1 sampling weight. Stage 2 uses Syn4D and MultiCamVideo for dynamic scenes and DL3DV and MVS-Synth for static scenes, increasing the dynamic share from 44.30%44.30\% to 70%70\%.

Table 9 lists the geometry and track source of each dataset (VGGT-Ω\Omega [5], CoWTracker [18], DepthAnything 3 [4]). The 30%30\% second-stage MultiCamVideo weight comprises 21%21\% dense and 9%9\% sparse query-frame data.

For static scenes, we form source–target pairs from different chunks of the same monocular video, similar to 4Real-Video-V2 [79]; temporal synchronization is unnecessary since the scene is static. Dynamic training pairs come from synchronized multiview videos; we do not use dynamic monocular videos for training.

Appendix D Camera-Adherence Evaluation on DAVIS

We construct our DAVIS evaluation set by selecting 5050 videos [80] and randomly sampling two target trajectories per video from the ReCamMaster [1] and Vista4D [11] trajectory pools. Baselines use released checkpoints and native generation resolutions; Vista4D uses 4RC-derived source geometry for this DAVIS comparison. We evaluate the first 4949 output frames. Camera recovery with VGGT-Ω\Omega and Pi3 uses 384×672384\times 672 frames; VBench uses the same resolution at 1616 FPS with each clip’s caption. The main Holo4D result uses 4RC source depth, cameras, and dense tracks, with 5050 denoising steps, CFG 55, shift 55, and seed 4242.

VGGT-Ω\Omega recovers cameras from generated videos. Translation metrics use the 5454 translation-bearing trajectories; rotation uses all 100100. DAVIS has no captured target-view reference for these paths, so we report camera control and VBench scores. All methods are evaluated with the same VGGT-Ω\Omega evaluator revision on all 100100 videos; baseline videos are the stored outputs of their released models, not resampled. For ATE and RPE-T, we anchor both trajectories at their first camera and rescale the predicted camera centers to match the centered Frobenius norm of the requested centers. We average per-video RMSEs; relative errors use adjacent frames. No subsequent global rotation alignment is applied to ATE, so orientation errors after the first frame contribute to it. Its magnitude also depends on the requested trajectories and is not directly comparable across DAVIS and Vista4D trajectory sets.

Table 12 evaluates the same checkpoint with the two-stage backend, where GMOS static/dynamic fusion fixes background identities in 3D. At 5050 steps, this condition lowers ATE from 1.657×10−21.657\times 10^{-2} to 0.719×10−20.719\times 10^{-2}, while its VBench scores are lower (Table 11). With this condition, 2525 denoising steps give a lower rotation error than 5050 (0.077∘0.077^{\circ} versus 0.101∘0.101^{\circ}). The 4RC condition uses its reconstructed trajectories directly, without GMOS preprocessing. A 5B model with a dense identity-target track condition (Wan2.2-TI2V-5B, generated at 704×1280704\times 1280 with 5050 steps) behaves like the 14B model: with 4RC it has ATE 1.464×10−21.464\times 10^{-2} and rotation error 0.116∘0.116^{\circ}, and the two-stage backend with GMOS lowers these to 0.608×10−20.608\times 10^{-2} and 0.105∘0.105^{\circ} (Table 12). The Holo4D-5B† row in Table 12 is a 5B variant trained on OmniWorld-DROID, MultiCamVideo, TartanAir, and Kubric, excluding Syn4D, MVS-Synth, and DL3DV. With the same source condition and 2525 steps, its errors (ATE 0.914×10−20.914\times 10^{-2}, rotation 0.106∘0.106^{\circ}) remain below those of Vista4D. It uses step 29,00029{,}000 and a dense track condition without persistent identities. It also differs from Holo4D-14B in backbone and track condition, so this comparison is not a controlled data ablation. The Pi3 columns use source-aligned camera recovery. All Holo4D variants have lower Pi3 translation error than Vista4D; only the 14B variant with VGGT-Ω\Omega at 2525 steps also has lower Pi3 rotation error.

Compatibility with a smaller backbone.

The geometric interface also applies to Wan2.2-TI2V-5B with a variant of the track condition (Table 12). At 704×1280704\times 1280 with 5050 denoising steps on DAVIS, replacing 4RC with the two-stage backend and GMOS reduces ATE from 1.464×10−21.464\times 10^{-2} to 0.608×10−20.608\times 10^{-2}, and on the nine-clip Syn4D comparison its source-aligned rotation error rises from 0.515∘0.515^{\circ} with ground-truth geometry to 0.885∘0.885^{\circ} with 4RC estimates (Table 14). Both trends match the 14B model.

Sampling time of the 5B model.

On one H200 with 5050 denoising steps and 4949 frames, Holo4D-5B generates a 704×1280704\times 1280 video in 202.0202.0 s on average, versus 417.4417.4 s for Holo4D-14B at 384×672384\times 672 and 495.0495.0 s for Vista4D at 384×672384\times 672 (plus 6.26.2 s of point-cloud rendering), averaged over the same 100100 Vista4D trajectory pairs; peak GPU memory is 76.376.3, 43.243.2, and 49.949.9 GiB, respectively. For these two configurations, the measured sampling time of the 5B model is about 2.1×2.1\times lower than that of the 14B model; because backbone, resolution, and track condition all differ, this is not a speedup under matched conditions. These are complete sampling times with precomputed source reconstruction from the 100100-pair evaluation runs, not the matched two-trajectory profiling in Table 24, so the 14B totals differ between the two measurements.

GMOS within the same reconstruction backend.

The shared trajectory representation supports foreground/background fusion without modifying the generator: for the two-stage backend, background points are held fixed in 3D while foreground points keep their tracked motion, and a foreground mask decides which is which. Our default 4RC condition uses no explicit fusion.

Table 13 compares two foreground masks within the same static/dynamic fusion of the two-stage backend: GMOS masks and masks derived from track motion. Both rows use the step-19,50019{,}500 checkpoint, the same VGGT-Ω\Omega and CoWTracker caches with first-frame queries, 5050 denoising steps at 384×672384\times 672, CFG 55, shift 55, and seed 4242; the saved sampling settings are otherwise identical. In both rows, background identities are fixed at their query-frame positions and foreground identities keep their tracked motion, so the comparison isolates the segmentation, not fusion versus no fusion. GMOS lowers the VGGT-Ω\Omega errors (ATE by 27%27\%, RPE-T by 15%15\%, RPE-R by 12%12\%) and the Pi3 rotation error by 3%3\%, while the Pi3 translation error is essentially unchanged. The GMOS row is the 5050-step VGGT-Ω\Omega row of Table 12. Figure 12 illustrates the fusion on one DAVIS sequence.

Appendix E Camera Adherence on Vista4D Trajectories

We additionally evaluate on the 110110 native Vista4D trajectories with both generated-only VGGT-Ω\Omega recovery and Vista4D’s source-aligned Pi3 protocol (Table 6). Vista4D uses the benchmark’s released Pi3 reconstruction, masks, and rendered inputs, whereas Holo4D uses 4RC or the two-stage backend. This preserves Vista4D’s native preprocessing and compares complete pipelines; it does not isolate the video generator as the source of performance differences. For the qualitative comparisons in Figures 3 and 16, baselines use their released sampling settings and the benchmark’s released Pi3 geometry where a point cloud is required; Vista4D videos are its official outputs. The VGGT-Ω\Omega and Pi3 evaluators recover cameras for scoring and are separate from the source reconstruction used for generation. With 4RC source geometry, Holo4D has lower RPE-T under VGGT-Ω\Omega and lower translation error under Pi3, but higher rotation error under both evaluators. VGGT-Ω\Omega evaluation follows the normalization in Appendix D. ATE and RPE-T have 110110 valid values for Holo4D with 4RC and 109109 each for Vista4D and the two-stage condition; RPE-R uses all 110110. These are per-method valid-metric counts, not a common-subset evaluation. Scale normalization requires non-degenerate requested and recovered camera paths; a completed video can therefore lack a valid translation metric. Vista4D’s Pi3 protocol reconstructs source and generated frames jointly, then aligns the source cameras by Sim⁡(3)\mathrm{Sim}(3).

The 4RC condition in Table 6 uses its reconstructed trajectories without mask-guided fusion and aligns the geometry to the released camera coordinate system with a per-video scalar depth factor. An alternative pointmap Sim⁡(3)\mathrm{Sim}(3) alignment of the same checkpoint and 4RC geometry reduces VGGT-Ω\Omega RPE-R from 1.142∘1.142^{\circ} to 0.348∘0.348^{\circ}, but increases Pi3 RotErr from 14.98∘14.98^{\circ} to 17.19∘17.19^{\circ}. Thus the source-condition comparison includes alignment effects, and the two evaluators disagree on this preprocessing change.

Additional geometry comparisons.

Section 4.4 analyzes the ground-truth and 4RC comparisons in Table 14. All rows use nine held-out Syn4D flying_group clips, with source camera 00 and target camera 11. Pi3 [28] recovers cameras jointly from source and generated frames. In the additional Pi3-source group, Holo4D constructs tracks from estimated depth and cameras using ground-truth 2D correspondences and visibility, whereas Vista4D uses its native Pi3 reconstruction. This partially oracle condition is distinct from both the full ground-truth and 4RC conditions. The 5B model is Wan2.2-TI2V-5B with a dense identity-target track condition, generated at 384×672384\times 672; its source-aligned rotation error with Pi3 geometry is 0.740∘0.740^{\circ}.

On Vista4D’s native trajectories, source replacement changes camera estimates, geometry, and coverage together. Separating generator sensitivity from reconstruction error would require running both methods with the same estimated geometry on these trajectories.

Conditioning signals in early checkpoints.

To ask whether richer geometric conditions repair rotation, we compare four separately trained 1.3B checkpoints that add rendered RGB-D, tracks, and multi-frame rendering to Plücker camera rays (Table 15). The Pi3 translation error decreases monotonically from 0.9870.987 to 0.6850.685 as conditions are added, whereas rotation error does not decrease; rendered RGB-D raises it by 2.33∘2.33^{\circ} (95% confidence interval [0.18∘,4.73∘][0.18^{\circ},4.73^{\circ}] over the 2020 pairs). These early checkpoints barely follow the requested rotation, so the experiment shows only that added geometric conditions improve translation more readily than rotation; it does not measure the rotation accuracy of the final model. All four Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B checkpoints are evaluated at step 3,0003{,}000, using the same 4RC reconstructions, 288×512×49288\times 512\times 49 outputs, and 5050 denoising steps. The 2020 pairs come from ten sources, five selected for rotation failures, with metrics as in Table 6.
